title: Salt Crystal Close-Up
oneLiner: Pour a pinch of salt and explore its tiny crystal landscape with your phone.

A dark background makes white salt pop.

title: Button on Fabric

Align the button slightly off-center.
Hold breath briefly when tapping the shutter.

title: Fork Tine Forest

title: Pencil Tip Horizon
oneLiner: Fill the frame with a sharpened pencil tip like a lone peak on the horizon.

title: Droplets on a Leaf
oneLiner: Find water droplets on a houseplant leaf and treat each bead as a tiny world.
details: Mist a plant lightly or wait after watering, then move close to a leaf with visible droplets. Shoot so one bead is sharp while others blur softly. The curve of the leaf can feel like rolling hills beneath glass spheres.

Hold the phone with both hands for stability.

title: Coin Stack Canyon
oneLiner: Stack a few coins and photograph them like a canyon wall of metal.
details: Stack three to six coins and shoot from the side at coin height. Crop tight so rims and dates feel monumental. A dark surface below can read as shadowed ground in your miniature scene.

Soft window light shows engraved detail.
Prop the stack against a book if it wobbles.

title: Spice Label Texture
oneLiner: Move in on a spice jar label until the print becomes an abstract tiny landscape.
details: Choose any jar from your kitchen and photograph the label as close as possible. Let letters blur into color blocks and texture. Rotate the jar to find a patch of type or pattern that feels like terrain on a map.

Wipe the glass before shooting.
Crop square afterward for a graphic look.

title: Desk Pebble Planet
oneLiner: Place one small pebble or stone on your desk and make it look planet-sized.
details: Use a pebble, marble, or small rock from a drawer or plant pot. Set it on a plain surface and shoot from pebble height with a wide empty background. Crop so the stone dominates and the desk fades into space.
tips: Use side light to show surface pits and shine.
Blur the background by moving closer to the stone.
Try a dark desk mat for a space-like feel.

title: Keys on the Counter
oneLiner: Lay your keys out and tell a small story about where your day might go.
details: Empty your pocket or bag and arrange your keys on a clean surface. Shoot from above or at a slight angle so rings, tags, and wear marks are visible. You do not need every key—just an honest slice of what you carry.

Overlap keys slightly for depth.
Use window light for soft shadows.

title: Wallet Flat Lay

Group items by color or size.
Leave a little empty space for breathing room.
constraint: No visible full card numbers or names.

title: Phone and Earbuds

details: Place your phone and earbuds together on a table or desk. Show cable tangle or neat coil—your choice tells the mood. Frame them as companions rather than a product shot, with everyday clutter cropped out.

Try a diagonal layout for energy.
Expose for the screen if it is on.

title: Pen Meets Notebook

Use soft light to avoid harsh page glare.
Crop tight on the corner of the page.

title: Pocket Miscellany

details: Think mints, lip balm, tissues, hair ties, or a spare battery—ordinary items only. Lay them out on a flat surface and shoot so each object reads clearly. The fun is in how random pieces become a portrait of your habits.

title: Sunglasses Resting
oneLiner: Photograph your sunglasses where you usually toss them at day's end.

Shoot slightly off-angle to reduce self-reflection.
Use folded arms to create leading lines.

title: Sanitizer and Tissue
oneLiner: Document the small hygiene items you keep within reach every day.
details: Set hand sanitizer, tissues, or wipes together on a clean surface. Keep labels generic in frame if you prefer privacy. Shoot simply—the story is preparedness tucked into ordinary life.

Use neutral background colors.

title: Change and Receipt

details: Lay coins and a folded receipt on a flat surface. Turn the receipt so store names are hidden if you wish. The contrast between shiny metal and soft paper tells a quiet everyday tale.

Leave one corner of the receipt curled.
Shoot close so texture shows.

title: Hot Meets Cold

details: Try a steaming mug next to a cold glass of water, or warm hands near a chilled can from the fridge. Shoot quickly while steam is visible if you use heat. The contrast should read clearly without staging anything elaborate.

Condensation on the cold item adds story.
Keep the setup on a stable table.

title: Rough Versus Smooth

Keep colors simple so texture carries the idea.
Align the boundary on a third line.

title: Big Beside Small
oneLiner: Put a large everyday object next to a tiny one and play with scale.
details: Try a mug beside a coin, or a shoe beside a sock. Place them on the same surface so size contrast is honest. Shoot from an angle that keeps both fully visible and clearly different in scale.

Eye-level often reads scale best.
Use a plain background to avoid confusion.

title: Light Against Dark
oneLiner: Compose one brightly lit object against a deeply shadowed background.
details: Place a light-colored item in a beam from a window or lamp and let the surroundings fall dark. Expose for the bright subject and let shadows go black if needed. The opposite tones should feel deliberate, not accidental.

Use a white or pale object for maximum contrast.
Tap exposure on the lit subject before recomposing.

title: Old Next to New

Use even light so wear shows in detail.

title: Full Versus Empty

title: Soft and Hard

title: Order Versus Chaos

title: One Bold Letter

title: Slippers by the Chair
oneLiner: Photograph slippers or socks waiting where you kick them off at home.
details: Place footwear where you naturally leave them—by a chair, bed, or rug. Shoot from standing height looking down or from floor level looking across. The scene should feel lived-in, not styled for a magazine.
tips: Pair items slightly askew for authenticity.
Include a bit of rug or floor texture.
Soft morning light works beautifully here.

title: Shelf With a Plant
oneLiner: Frame a shelf where books and a houseplant share the same cozy ledge.
details: Choose one shelf or windowsill with a plant and a few books or trinkets. Balance the plant on a third and let leaves soften hard edges. Keep the shot about quiet domestic order, not a full room tour.
tips: Dust the shelf lip before shooting.
Use window side light on leaves.
Vertical phone orientation suits tall plants.
constraint: Include at least one book and one plant.

title: Window Seat Pause
oneLiner: Shoot the view from a window seat or sill with cushion and glass in frame.
details: Compose so the cushion or ledge occupies the foreground and the window glass leads outward. Weather outside does not matter—overcast, sun, or night all work. The cozy part is the seat; the world outside is secondary.
tips: Clean smudges on the glass you include.
Expose for the interior so outside may blow out.
Include a folded blanket if you have one.
constraint: Foreground must show fabric or cushion texture.

title: Candle and Closed Book
oneLiner: Set an unlit candle beside a closed book for a calm evening tableau.
details: Arrange a candle and book on a tray or table—no need to light the candle. Add a pen or reading glasses if they are already nearby. Shoot warm and close so the scene feels like a breath before bedtime.
tips: Unlit candles are safer and still read cozy.
Match book and candle heights for balance.
Use lamp light, not harsh overhead flash.
constraint: Do not light the candle—photograph it unlit.

title: Ceiling Light Halo
oneLiner: Stand beneath a ceiling fixture and shoot upward into its glow.
details: Find a pendant, flush mount, or fan light indoors and point the camera straight up. Include the ceiling radius around the fixture for context. Watch exposure so the bulb does not blow out entirely unless you want a star burst.
tips: Hold the phone steady with both hands.
Try slightly off-center composition.
Clean the fixture if dust webs show.
constraint: Camera must point within thirty degrees of straight up.

title: Houseplant From Ground
oneLiner: Lay the phone low and photograph a houseplant as if you were an ant looking up.
details: Place your phone on the floor or a low stool aimed up through the leaves toward light. Trunks, stems, and leaf silhouettes should tower overhead. A window or lamp behind the plant adds drama.
tips: Use pro mode or tap focus on nearest leaves.
Wipe the floor area so it is not in sharp detail.
Shoot portrait orientation for height.

title: Under the Table View
oneLiner: Slide low and shoot upward at a table or desk from underneath its edge.
details: Kneel or place the phone on the floor near a table and aim up at the underside and top surface. Legs, books, or a mug rim can silhouette against the ceiling. Keep the angle clearly from below, not eye level.
tips: Use a self-timer to avoid awkward bending.
Include at least two table legs for structure.
Expose for the brighter ceiling.
constraint: Camera height must be below the table surface.

title: Staircase Underside
oneLiner: From the bottom step, shoot upward along the railing and climbing treads.
details: Stand on the lowest step and point the camera up the stairwell. Lines of treads and banisters should converge toward the top landing. Include a slice of ceiling or upper wall to sell the height.
tips: Keep verticals straight with grid lines.
Shoot when the stairwell is empty of people.
Use available house lights—no flash needed.
constraint: Start from the lowest step you can safely reach.

title: Tree Canopy Cathedral
oneLiner: Lie or crouch beneath a tree and shoot up through branches toward the sky.
details: Find any accessible tree and aim upward so trunk and branches frame the sky. Leaves can be dense or sparse—both work. The trunk should anchor a corner while branches radiate outward like a vault.
tips: Use burst mode if wind moves leaves.
Polarized look is optional—just avoid shooting into sun glare.
Include only sky and tree—no buildings required.

title: Tower From the Sidewalk
oneLiner: Stand at the base of a building and shoot straight up along its facade.
details: Choose any multistory building you can view from a public sidewalk. Point upward so walls, windows, and edges converge. Keep faces out of the frame entirely.
tips: Center the corner for strong leading lines.
Watch for security rules on private courtyards.
Expose for the building, not the sky hole.
constraint: Building lines must converge toward the top of frame.

title: Sky Between Buildings
oneLiner: Frame a slice of sky sandwiched between upper walls or building tops.
details: From street or yard level, aim up until walls or upper stories border the sky on both sides. The sky becomes a bright ribbon and the architecture feels towering. Clouds or clear blue both suit the prompt.
tips: Rotate phone for a vertical sky strip.
Keep wires minimal if possible.
Step back if walls do not align—perspective helps.
constraint: Sky must be bordered by architecture on at least two sides.
